articles.text: The Indians near Lawndale, Pratt Co., Kansas are on the war-path and have killed several settlers.
articles.summary: Indians near Lawndale, Kansas, reported on the war-path.

articles.text: The English cabinet has decided not to declare what its foreign policy will be. Lord Salisbury says that in reference to Russia, Gladstone's policy will be carried out.
articles.summary: English cabinet's foreign policy under Salisbury.

articles.text: Bradlaugh, the atheist who was returned by the electors of Northampton and has repeatedly tried to take his seat in the house of Commons, was again refused permission to take the oath of office.
articles.summary: Bradlaugh again refused the oath in the House of Commons.

articles.text: Samuel T. Hauser, of Helena, has been appointed governor of Montana. The appointment has called forth many expressions of commendation, Mr. Hauser being a prominent business man of Helena.
articles.summary: Samuel T. Hauser of Helena appointed governor of Montana.

articles.text: The hotel Ryan, at St Paul, one of the largest in the United States, is now open and has created havoc among the other hotels and restaurants. The Metropolitan and Brevoort cafe have closed permanently.
articles.summary: Hotel Ryan opens at St. Paul.

articles.text: All the West division street car employes in Chicago have been on a strike for the last week, causing great inconvenience to the traveling public. The matter is now being arbitrated and the men have gone back to work.
articles.summary: Chicago West division street car strike.

articles.text: Gov. Pierce has given notice that the senate committee on Indian affairs, senator Harrison presiding, will visit the Crow creek and Winnebago reservations the 16th. and 17th., to try and adjust difficulties with the settlers.
articles.summary: Senate Indian affairs committee to visit Crow Creek and Winnebago reservations.

articles.text: Mr. Leo Welz, a nursery man in Ohio, has been authorized by the department of agriculture to purchase in Russia as many varieties of all kinds of fruit trees as in his opinion will grow in the northwest. We hope that this move will be successful as Dakota is not now blessed with a large variety of fruit trees.
articles.summary: Leo Welz to buy Russian fruit trees for the northwest.

articles.text: The number of tramps on the road seems to be increasing year by year and their nerve increases with their numbers. Not more than half will do any work to pay for food. We call upon every citizen not to give a tramp a bite to eat until he has earned it. This is the best way of ridding ourselves of the pests.
articles.summary: Editorial urging citizens not to feed tramps who will not work.

articles.text: A riot was narrowly averted on the 4th. at Salt Lake City. The Mormons, not content with living in open defiance of the law, placed all flags on public buildings at half-mast. After much trouble they were either lowered completely or run up to the masthead. Such an evidence of treason should receive cordign punishment.
articles.summary: Near-riot at Salt Lake City over flags at half-mast on the Fourth.

articles.text: The bids for territorial bonds were opened Tuesday at Bismarck. The total amount of bonds to be issued is $176,000 and are for the penal, charitable and educational institutions of Dakota. There were ten bidders Preston & Co., of Chicago, bidding 3 1-5 per cent. premium will probably get the award. The bonds are to draw six per cent. interest and the credit of the territory must be high to call for such large bids.
articles.summary: Bids for $176,000 in Dakota territorial bonds opened at Bismarck.

articles.text: Ex-Gov. Mc Cook, of Colorado, comes out in a letter, declaring the Indian leases in Indian territory to be illegal. Under the law, the secretary of the Interior has full control of Indian affairs, subject to direction by the President. No purchase, grant. lease or other conveyance of land can be made except by treaty or convention, according to the constitution. The United States alone can make a contract with the Indians for their lands. Gen. McCook quotes the law to substantiate the above points. He also states that nearly 9,000,000 acres have been leased by different individuals and corporations from the Indians all of which leases are illegal. General McCook farther states that in many instances the present lessees of the land are foreigners who have no other interests in the United States. He also shows that only a few acres per capita are left to the Indians, not enough for each to have a respectable farm. It seems strange, if all Gen. McCook says is true, that such a state of things could exist. How the matter will end is problematical, but it seems now as though the leases in Indian territory must be given up. If so, it will greatly enhance the value of our northwestern grazing lands.
articles.summary: Ex-Gov. McCook says Indian Territory leases are illegal; their end would raise value of northwestern grazing lands.

articles.text: Charlie Eaton was in from his ranch Saturday and stated that the grasshoppers have seriously injured the southern Yellowstone ranges. In many cases it will be difficult for the cattle to obtain sufficient feed.
articles.summary: Charlie Eaton reports grasshoppers have damaged the southern Yellowstone ranges.

articles.text: Mr. Shaw, of Dayton, Washington Territory, passed through Sunday evening with two cars of horses and a car of mules for Mr. Larson, twenty miles south of Jamestown. One car of horses were all Morgans and as fine a lot as were ever shipped through Medora. They were bred by Mr. Shaw who states that Morgans are taking the lead over all other horses combined in Washington.
articles.summary: Mr. Shaw of Dayton, W. T., ships Morgan horses and mules through Medora.

articles.text: The receipts of cattle at the Chicago stock-yards numbered 41,088 head this week. Prices dropped 25@40c. for native steers and 10@25c. for other grades. Foreign prices are firm and higher for good to choice American cattle. There were plenty of medium and inferior cattle on the market but fewer choice to fancy than the preceding week. 9,000 Texans were received, making about 30,000 during the last three weeks. Texan bulls sold as low as $2.25; fair to good steers, $3@3.40; Indian territory cattle $4@4.60. The market was firm with higher tendency Tuesday.
articles.summary: Chicago stock-yards receipts and prices for the week.

articles.text: A popular amusement among cattlemen is guessing at the weight of animals. Some of the guesses are remarkably accurate. A case has recently been noted where two men guessed at the live weight of 1,075 cattle, each marking his guess on a slip of paper. On comparisons their guesses were found to be within a hundred and fifty pounds of each other and when the cattle were weighed the higher guess was found to be within five pounds of the true weight. Guessing how much cattle will dress out is a much harder task, the most authentic instance being the guess of John Deffebach. He guessed at the dressed weight of fifteen head of cattle and came within five pounds of the weight. This guess is authenticated by Rassie and Levi Deffebach and a large number of men in Central City.
articles.summary: Guessing cattle weights; John Deffebach's accurate guess of dressed weight.

articles.text: It is safe to assume that a year or two more will see the Bad Lands as full of range cattle as will be profitable, taking into consideration the natural increase and the additions to the present herds. The question of quantity, or having as many cattle on the range as is safe, is, therefore, on the point of solving itself. The question of quality, however, has by no means had a sufficient share of the general attention. It has been proved so conclusively that it pays to raise grade cattle instead of scrubs that we will leave that point unnoticed and look for the cheapest and best way to raise a higher class of cattle. Of course this is done by using a better class of bulls but it seems to us that in the way of getting these bulls a large amount of money is spent that could be saved. Nine out of every ten ranchmen send east after bulls that could be raised to far better advantage here. It is not necessary for every cowman to have a full-blood herd but it would be an extremely profitable business for men of means to start such a herd in the range country. This would by no means be an experiment as it has been successfully tried in the south and to some extent in the west. By this means, there would be a large saving in three ways: transportation from the east here, an absence of the heavy loss occasioned by acclimatization and the comparative cheapness of raising cattle here to the cost in the east. These three reasons certainly make the cost of each animal $20 more. The range breeder therefore, could undersell the eastern breeder by this amount and make the same profit. Added to this would be readier sales owing to nearness to the market and the greater and acknowledged superiority of range-raised bulls. Who will be the man to accept this opportunity?
articles.summary: Editorial urging range breeding of full-blood bulls in the Bad Lands instead of shipping bulls from the east.

articles.text: If any one wants to realize the true get-there-ativeness of the English language, he should be on hand about the third or fourth time the cattle break when they are being corrailed for slaughtering.

articles.text: It may be fun for the tenderfeet but it must be annoying to the steers to have their hides riddled with bullets if one happens to break away from the bunch. One shot is as good as fifty if put in the right place.

articles.text: Rassie Deffebach has been engaged by M. Wadsworth as foreman for the Bad Lands cattle Co., and will to-morrow remove his family to Dickinson, this point being more accessible to Wadsworth's line camp. We are sorry to see them leave and Dickinson can congratulate herself on having a very pleasant family added to her citizens.

articles.text: Mr. Van Brunt, president of the VI cattle Co., left for his home in Milwaukee after a six weeks' visit. He is greatly pleased with the condition of the cattle and has enjoyed the round-up hugely. He has also established a reputation as a host that will be long in fading away. Not a solitary VI bull died last winter, every animal having been rounded up.
articles.summary: VI Cattle Co. president Van Brunt leaves after six weeks' visit.

articles.text: It has passed the funny or amusing point when persons indulge in such promiscuous shooting as was done the night of July 4. Of course there is no objection to a reasonable amount of jollity on that day, but when anyone persists in shooting far into the night and in the immediate vicinity of hotels, where people desire to sleep, it is time that the foolishness was stopped. Not content with keeping would-be sleepers on this side the river awake, a gang went over the river Saturday night and shooting unexpectedly near the Pyramid Park hotel, where Joe McCoul is lying with a broken leg, gave him such a start that he labored under intense pain all night and until the doctor came in the morning. It was Joe's opinion and that of his watchers, that his leg was broken again. Happily, this did not prove to be the case. Acting under full authority, therefore, and with the full concurrence of all good citizens, Fred. Willard has published the notice in this issue that the law will be strictly enforced in reference to promiscuous shooting.
articles.summary: Editorial against promiscuous shooting on the Fourth; shots near Pyramid Park hotel disturbed injured Joe McCoul.

articles.headline: Fourth of July Sports.
articles.text:
The sport on the 4th., although interrupted by the rain, which fell at frequent intervals, was much enjoyed.

In the morning a game of base-ball was begun which, on account of the rain only lasted three innings. The game served to develop the fact that we have a number of good players here. The nines were chosen, as near as possible, one from the slaughter-house and one from the town. At the finish the score was a tie, two to two.

The first race of the afternoon was the fat men's race, won in a canter by Ed Myers, the fairy sylph who officiates at the slaughter-house scales. Sam Whitney and MacDonald ran a close race for second, Sam finally winning, while Shorty, the gazelle-built manipulator of buffalo horns was distanced, he having tripped on a blade of grass or some other obstruction.

Putting Bob Roberts' mule outfit into requisition the hole Shorty made in the ground was soon filled up and the ground again smoothed for the 600 yard race, the event of the day. For this there were only four starters, the slippery track deterring many from the dangers of such a race. The starters were Blue Jay entered by Van Eeghan, Splinter and Lengthy by Goodall and Fox by Van Driesche. It looked like a clear walk-away for Blue Jay, who was freely backed against the field. The slippery track, however, upset the calculations of every one and the dark horse won, Splinter coming in a good two lengths ahead of Lengthy, who was closely followed by Blue Jay and Fox. Splinter ran a splendid race, carrying Mose Ryder and a heavy California saddle, the two weighing at least two hundred and sixty pounds. Contrary to expectations, Fox made a brilliant race. He is only four years old and is not fairly broken but he lapped Blue Jay at the finish.

The next event was a hundred yard foot race, arranged on the ground between Joe Houston and Walter Watterson. It was a close and exciting race, Joe coming in about a foot ahead. An animated discussion arising over the decision of this race it was decided to have a repetition in the regular hundred yard race.

For the hundred yards' race there were nine starters and for the number starting was a remarkably even race. It was won by Pat. Moore. Houston again beat Watterson, though neither secured a place in the race. The last race was the free-for-all three hundred yard horse race and it is seldom that a prettier finish is witnessed. There were only two entries: Gopher by Van Eeghan and Topsy by Goodall. Topsy lapped Gopher all through the race but could not get his nose ahead of the horse on whom every boy on the river will "go broke" if anything can beat him. Gopher was not struck a blow during the race, seeming to know that he was only required to keep ahead.

Johnny Goodall captured the bulk of the prizes, walking away with the remnants of $65, the remainder gracing the till of Bob. Roberts' wet goods hostelry.

The money for the purses was easily raised by subscription and had it not been for the rain, nothing would have marred the day's entertainment.

At the close of the racing, a boxing-match was held in Roberts' hall. Although the result was one-sided it showed that Medora certainly possesses her share of "talent."
articles.summary: Medora's Fourth of July sports: a rain-shortened ball game, foot races and horse races (Splinter won the 600 yards), and a boxing match in Roberts' hall.

articles.text:
Brand: E. W. Casey, Frank S. Moore, Manager, P.O. Medora, Billings Co., Dak. — KC on left shoulder, F on left hip; 2nd brand same without circle; range O'Donnell creek
Brand: Sloping Bottom Ranch, Lloyd Roberts, Proprietor, P.O. Medora — brand on left hip; range Little Missouri 7 miles south of N. P. R. R.; horse brand same on left shoulder
Brand: Badger Cattle Company, Howard Eaton, M'g'r, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — VI on left hip, horse brand same; range Beaver creek and Little Missouri river
Brand: Dorr Clark, Spearfish, Dakota — VVV on left side; ear mark under-bit in left ear; range Belle Fourche
Brand: Clark & Plum, Spearfish, Dakota — E6 on left side; ear mark left ear cropped; range Grand river; additional brands ZD, DZ, ZD (bar), circle cross; $100 reward re VVV or E6 ranges
Brand: Little Missouri Horse Company, [?] Tarbell, M'n'g'r, Medora — H on left shoulder; range Davis creek and Little Missouri river
Brand: W. N. Thompson & Co., Wm. Dantz, Manager, P.O. Medora — quarter-circle diamond TD on left hip; vent bar under T. D.; ear mark tip of left ear cut off square
Brand: Lemoyne Cattle Co. (Limited), D. K. Wade, Manager, Medora — LC on left side, reversed C on right hip; range Little Missouri south of the R. R.; ranch Tepee bottom; owners of DW brand
Brand: Soho Cattle Co., Chas. Eaton, Manager, Medora — SO on left side; range Little Missouri river and Beaver creek, north of N. P. R. R.
Brand: Chimney Butte Ranch, Theodore Roosevelt, Proprietor; Ferris & Merrifield, Managers; P.O. Medora — Maltese cross on left hip or right side; down cut dewlap; range six miles south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri
Brand: Bullion Creek Horse Ranch, Jack Bullion, Prop., Medora — 55 on left hip; range Bullion creek, twenty miles south of Medora
Brand: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., Medora — several cattle brands on left side (incl. circle JP and others); also steers purchased of Mason & Lovell; range Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: Spring Creek Ranch, L. D. & B. Rumsey, J. L. Truscott, Manager, P.O. Medora — circle-R-circle-B on left hip and side; ear marks both ears swallow forked; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri
Brand: Berry, Boice & Co., P.O. Keith, Montana — 777 on right hip, side and shoulder; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: E. G. Paddock, P.O. Medora — six-inch circle-dot on both sides; range six miles north of crossing of N. P. R. R. and Little Missouri; horses four-inch circle-dot on left shoulder and left hip
Brand: Lydia S. Fuller, Frank S. Moore, Manager, P.O. Medora — LSF on left shoulder; range O'Donnell creek
Brand: Custer Trail Cattle Co., A. Alden Eaton, Supt., P.O. Medora — HK in circle on left side; range Little Missouri river, Deep and Davis creeks
Brand: Towers & Gudgell, P.O. Keith, Montana — brand on right side, additional V; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: Bad Lands Cattle Co., M. Wadsworth, Manager, P.O. Medora — 71 on right hip and shoulder, bellows, Pd brands; range Little Missouri fifteen miles north of Medora
Brand: Neimmela Ranch, Gregor Lang, Manager, P.O. Medora — thistle and other brands; range Keogh crossing of Little Missouri to Pretty butte
